article.title: FCC Adds Foreign-Made Humanoid Robots and Power Inverters to Covered List, Targeting China's Market Lead
article.summary: The FCC barred new foreign-made humanoid and quadruped robots and power inverters from U.S. authorization over national security risks, a move aimed chiefly at China.
article.body_markdown:
## Overview

The Federal Communications Commission added foreign-produced humanoid and quadruped robots, along with foreign-produced power inverters, to its "Covered List" of equipment barred from new FCC authorization, according to the [FCC's own fact sheet](https://docs.fcc.gov/public/attachments/DOC-423682A1.txt). The update, released July 28, 2026 and reported the following day, blocks new models of these devices from being imported, marketed, or sold in the United States, and lands squarely on China, which dominates global humanoid robot production.

## What We Know

The FCC's fact sheet defines the newly covered "advanced robotic devices" as mobile robots, "such as humanoids and quadrupeds," a definition corroborated by [Robotics and Automation News](https://roboticsandautomationnews.com/2026/07/29/fcc-updates-covered-list-to-include-foreign-produced-advanced-robotic-devices-and-power-inverters/103658/). The determination that these products and foreign-produced connected power inverters "pose unacceptable risks to the national security of the United States or the safety and security of United States persons" came from a White House-convened Executive Branch interagency body with national security expertise, not from the FCC itself, per the [fact sheet](https://docs.fcc.gov/public/attachments/DOC-423682A1.txt).

FCC Chairman Brendan Carr said, "Following President Trump's leadership, the FCC will continue to do our part to secure America's critical supply chains and, with today's action, the FCC is acting in lock step with our national security agencies to do just that," according to the [FCC's fact sheet](https://docs.fcc.gov/public/attachments/DOC-423682A1.txt), a statement also reported verbatim by [Gizmodo](https://gizmodo.com/white-house-bans-foreign-humanoid-robots-in-bid-to-slow-chinas-tech-explosion-2000792090) and [Route Fifty](https://www.route-fifty.com/cybersecurity/2026/07/fcc-blocks-approval-new-foreign-made-robots-power-inverters/415078/). Route Fifty also reported that an unnamed FCC official said "remote connectivity capabilities built into many of the devices create inherent security vulnerabilities," warning that foreign entities could use inverter access to "disable equipment, steal data, conduct surveillance, or launch cyberattacks," while networked robots could be manipulated in their "data and physical operation." [CBS News](https://www.cbsnews.com/news/humanoid-robots-imports-us-ban-china-national-security-concerns/) reported the underlying concern in similar terms: that advanced robotic devices could "collect data leveraged by malign actors to surveil Americans, enhance foreign intelligence capabilities, or to remotely commandeer the robots."

The restriction is not retroactive. Previously authorized robot and inverter models already on the market are unaffected, and federal government purchases are exempt, according to the [FCC fact sheet](https://docs.fcc.gov/public/attachments/DOC-423682A1.txt) and [Gizmodo](https://gizmodo.com/white-house-bans-foreign-humanoid-robots-in-bid-to-slow-chinas-tech-explosion-2000792090). Manufacturers can still seek a "Conditional Approval" exemption: for robots, that approval must come from the Department of War (DoW), and for power inverters, from either the Department of War or the Department of Homeland Security, per the [FCC fact sheet](https://docs.fcc.gov/public/attachments/DOC-423682A1.txt) and [Route Fifty](https://www.route-fifty.com/cybersecurity/2026/07/fcc-blocks-approval-new-foreign-made-robots-power-inverters/415078/), which also noted that applications go through a dedicated conditional-approvals email address. Route Fifty added that the Covered List previously targeted specific companies such as Huawei and ZTE, and that this update marks an expansion to entire categories of devices regardless of the manufacturer's country of origin.

The rule targets a market China clearly leads. China holds roughly 85% of the global humanoid robot market, according to both [CBS News](https://www.cbsnews.com/news/humanoid-robots-imports-us-ban-china-national-security-concerns/) and [American Bazaar](https://americanbazaaronline.com/2026/07/29/fcc-announces-ban-on-foreign-humanoid-robots-targeting-china-485439/), which both reported that roughly 15,000 humanoid robots shipped globally in 2025, with Chinese firms Unitree and AGIBOT each shipping more than 5,000 units while U.S. rivals Tesla and Figure AI shipped a few hundred units or fewer. Both outlets also cited a Morgan Stanley forecast that China's humanoid robot market could reach $15 billion by 2030. [American Bazaar](https://americanbazaaronline.com/2026/07/29/fcc-announces-ban-on-foreign-humanoid-robots-targeting-china-485439/) and [CBS News](https://www.cbsnews.com/news/humanoid-robots-imports-us-ban-china-national-security-concerns/) both reported that the Pentagon has listed Unitree, along with other major Chinese technology companies, as having alleged ties to the Chinese military — a claim Beijing has rejected.

China's Foreign Ministry pushed back through spokesperson Mao Ning, who told reporters that protectionism would not make the United States more competitive and would instead hurt American businesses and consumers, according to [CBS News](https://www.cbsnews.com/news/humanoid-robots-imports-us-ban-china-national-security-concerns/) and [CGTN](https://news.cgtn.com/news/2026-07-29/China-opposes-US-restrictions-on-foreign-made-advanced-robots-1PaSAY86YKs/p.html). Mao said China has consistently opposed what it characterizes as Washington's misuse of national security justifications to target Chinese companies, and pledged that Beijing would take the measures necessary to defend the legitimate interests of Chinese firms, per [CGTN](https://news.cgtn.com/news/2026-07-29/China-opposes-US-restrictions-on-foreign-made-advanced-robots-1PaSAY86YKs/p.html). [American Bazaar](https://americanbazaaronline.com/2026/07/29/fcc-announces-ban-on-foreign-humanoid-robots-targeting-china-485439/) and [CBS News](https://www.cbsnews.com/news/humanoid-robots-imports-us-ban-china-national-security-concerns/) reported that the restrictions arrive ahead of a planned September 2026 summit between President Trump and Chinese leader Xi Jinping, a meeting American Bazaar described as a potential flashpoint given the new trade friction.

## What We Don't Know

None of the sources reviewed specify an exact date on which the interagency national security determinations underlying the rule were formally transmitted to the FCC, only that the Covered List update itself was released July 28, 2026. It is also unclear how many pending robot or inverter authorization applications, if any, are currently caught in limbo awaiting a Conditional Approval decision from the Department of War or Department of Homeland Security, or how quickly that exemption process is expected to move.

## Analysis

The order extends a national security framework the FCC has used for years against specific companies like Huawei and ZTE, per [Route Fifty](https://www.route-fifty.com/cybersecurity/2026/07/fcc-blocks-approval-new-foreign-made-robots-power-inverters/415078/), into an entire emerging product category just as humanoid robots move from research demos into commercial deployment. Because the restriction is framed around country-neutral device categories rather than named companies, it technically applies to any foreign manufacturer — but given China's roughly 85% share of global humanoid robot shipments, the practical effect falls almost entirely on Chinese suppliers such as Unitree and AGIBOT, right as both companies compete for a market Morgan Stanley expects to be worth billions of dollars within the decade.
